title: Draft one
hook: gather your pages into one short rule: Sariputta begs the Buddha to lay down rules, and the Buddha says wait
tomorrow: a man swore to do the basics, no more, no less. was that enough?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: my season. Benedict's Rule moved with the year, and on a stormy night love outranked the clock. Today, all your pages become one first draft, on one page.

A new notebook, and the urge to write the perfect plan before living a single day of it. The Buddha's disciple Sariputta had a version of that urge. At a place called Verañja, he asks the Buddha: why did the teaching of some Buddhas of the past last a long time, while others faded? Because some laid down training rules for their followers, the Buddha says, and some didn't. Then lay them down now, Sariputta says. He isn't being fussy; he wants the teaching to last. And here's the odd part. The Buddha says: wait.
screen: `THE PERFECT PLAN, FIRST.` → `WHY DID SOME TEACHINGS LAST?` → `LAY DOWN THE RULES NOW.` → `THE BUDDHA SAYS: WAIT.`

segments.voice: Wait, Sariputta. The Teacher will know the time. A rule isn't laid down until the trouble it's for actually shows up in the community. In the Vinaya's telling, that's how the Buddhist monastic code grew. Not as a manual written in advance, but one case at a time. Something happens, someone is harmed or confused, it's brought to the Buddha, and a rule is made, with the story often kept beside it. That's why the Vinaya reads partly like a book of stories: a training rule usually comes with its origin. The Patimokkha, the list monks and nuns recite together, is the gathered result. It wasn't drafted in a quiet room; it was collected from life. Here's the teaching, named plainly: in Buddhism, a rule answers real life. It's built from what actually happened, then refined as more happens. A rule of your own can grow the same way. You've already written the pages: the body, the people, study, the breaking rule, the season. Draft one doesn't invent a new life. It gathers what months of practice already showed you, and puts it on one page. The perfect version can wait. The real one starts from what's there.
screen: `WAIT: THE TEACHER KNOWS THE TIME.` · `ONE CASE AT A TIME.` · `EVERY RULE HAS ITS STORY.` · `GATHER WHAT YOU'VE LIVED.` · then, large: `DRAFT ONE.`

segments.voice: Gather your pages: the body, the people, study, the breaking rule, the season. On one fresh sheet, by hand, write the line from each page you've actually kept, not the one you wish you'd kept. If a page has nothing kept, leave its line blank; that tells you something too. Then sit with the page on your lap for the rest of the time.
Draft one: your pages gathered into one short rule, built from what actually happened, the way the Vinaya grew, one case at a time.

howItsDone: The Buddhist monastic code, the Vinaya, records each training rule with the case that led to it; the gathered rules, the Patimokkha, are recited by monks and nuns on observance days. A personal rule of life is often drafted the same way: from what has actually been kept.
